subject: strandbeest
pitch:
Category: Abstract.
Subject: wind-walking beach creature of tubes.
Style: Theo Jansen kinetic sculpture.
reasoning:
I'm thinking through a Strandbeest-style walking creature built from yellow PVC tubes with Jansen linkage legs and wind-catching sails, aiming for roughly 250 parts with a rigged joint structure. I'm scaling it to be plausible, close to real Strandbeest proportions around 1.8-2m tall.

Now I'm working out the Jansen leg mechanism geometry using the classic "holy numbers" for rod lengths, setting up fixed pivot points and crank positions, then computing the intersecting circle constraints to solve for each linkage joint position relative to the crank angle.

I'm still working through the exact linkage distances, but since getting every value precisely right is tricky, I'll make sure the circle-intersection logic has a clamping fallback so the mechanism still renders even if some distances don't perfectly intersect.

Let me try hardcoding a known Jansen linkage pose instead, computing the intersection points by hand with Q at a specific crank angle to get concrete triangulated coordinates for N1 using the distance formula.

Given the uncertainty in picking the correct side for each joint, I'll build a generic solver that intersects circles for each linkage point and lets me specify a sign parameter per joint to choose the correct branch, since I can't fully verify the geometry by hand under this time pressure.

I'm working through the exact linkage lengths from the Jansen mechanism diagram, trying to map which triangle each side belongs to (b, c, d forming the fixed triangle P-A-B, then j, k, e connecting to the crank and next joints). It's a bit fiddly matching labeled lengths to the correct node pairs, so I'm carefully cross-checking each triangle's three sides against known values before moving to the next linkage segment.

Actually, let me simplify to 9 bars and work out coordinates directly: placing A upper-left relative to the frame pivot P, then locating B from the known distances off both P and A.

Checking perpendicular options for B, I pick the leftward solution since Q sits to the right, giving B at roughly (-37.2, 12.5), and now I'm setting up triangle constraints to find C using its distances to B and Q.

Continuing from B, the foot lands near (27.9,-59.4), giving a leg height around 59 units from P, which seems reasonable. I'll need to scale this down—maybe by a factor of 0.016—to get realistic dimensions in meters.

For implementing the solver, I'm designing a generic circle-intersection function that takes two points, two radii, and a sign flag to pick between the two possible intersection points, with clamping to handle edge cases. Then I'm working out the perpendicular direction conventions for each joint (A, B, C, D) based on the direction vectors between consecutive points, choosing signs to get the geometrically correct leg configuration.

I'm also mapping the 2D linkage coordinates into 3D model space, deciding that x maps to forward (z) direction with each leg assembly living in a fixed side-offset plane, and thinking through how Jansen's mechanism typically uses paired/doubled legs per side that I'll need to replicate for the strandbeest structure.

I'm planning the leg layout with 3 units per side spaced along z, phased 0/120/240 degrees with inner/outer plane pairs per side, giving 12 leg planes total each needing roughly 9 rods plus crank and nodes — around 250 parts overall, which should be manageable.

Now I'm detailing the rods as thin yellow tubes between node points with small connector caps, and sketching the rigging: a root hips joint, spine chain, crank axle joints per unit, and simplified per-leg joint chains so the rods can attach cleanly to bones.

I'm building the chain as a polyline through points P, C, D to form the leg tip. For the chassis I'm thinking through Jansen's linkage structure: the real mechanism has a crankshaft running along x per side, with legs living in planes perpendicular to that axle, so I need one transverse axle per unit z position carrying the crank.

I'm placing three axles across the body, each spanning x from -0.8 to 0.8 with left and right leg phases offset 180 degrees for alternating gait, and attaching crank arms of the correct length from the axle center to the moving joint. I still need to work out where the fixed pivot point sits relative to the crank center, since that offset determines how the whole frame rail aligns with each unit.

I realize the feet extend far enough to overlap neighboring units in the same lateral plane, so I need each unit to stagger its lateral offset slightly to avoid visual collisions between adjacent legs.

I'm widening unit 1's lateral base relative to units 0 and 2, checking leg lengths against the spacing between units to confirm no overlap, then sketching a central spine chassis with cross braces connecting down to the axles, and working out the foot's vertical position relative to the body.

Instead of hardcoding the body height, I'll solve all leg phases first, find the minimum foot y-position across the gait cycle, and shift the whole body up so that point plus a small foot-cap sphere radius just touches the floor.

For the walking gait, I'll offset left and right leg phases by 180° so feet alternate naturally. Now I'm thinking about adding the Jansen wind-catching mechanism — a mast with weathered sailcloth and a row of translucent bottle bladders along the rails, which is such an iconic visual element of these kinetic sculptures.

I'll include a simplified spine chain with a front "head"-like sail-vane joint instead of a literal jaw, since this creature is abstract. For scale, I'm setting the legs and chassis so the overall height lands around 2.6m with the mast reaching up to 2.5m, matching real Jansen sculptures. For color, I'm going with a sun-bleached yellow PVC tone with weathering variation rather than flat paint.

Now I'm working out the material details: yellow tube paint that blends toward sandy tones near the base, with scuff noise added, plus translucent white-blue bladders, black zip-tie connectors, dark rubber joint caps, and tan rigging ropes from mast to chassis. For the sails, I'm deciding to use a membrane surface between curve edges rather than a flat textured plane, since that lets me paint seam lines along and across the cloth, and I'm setting up the membrane to stretch from the mast edge to the boom edge.

I'm also sketching out some charming decorative touches -- painted "eyes" on the front bladders with sclera and pupil detail, a wave/spiral emblem painted on the sail, and maybe a small pennant flag -- planning to build these as a few SVG textures (eye, sail mark, flag) before moving into actual coding.

Now I'm working out the geometry for the leg mechanism -- defining a circle-intersection helper to find where two circles meet given their centers and radii, then using it to solve the leg linkage positions by chaining these intersections through several pivot points.

I'm mapping out the full rod structure (eight linkage rods plus the crank and the chassis frame piece), then starting to figure out how to project these 2D leg coordinates into the 3D model space.

Now I'm sizing the rod radii and node geometry, planning small cylinders at each joint to represent the pivot points across the multiple leg planes.

I'm roughly tallying parts per leg plane (rods, nodes, foot) and multiplying across all twelve planes plus chassis components to get a total part-count estimate before writing the rod-bone helper function.

Now I'm thinking through the skeleton rig: giving each crank axle its own hinge joint with rigid crank arms, attaching leg chains to a parent spine joint, and laying out the root hips joint and spine chain positions along the body.

I'm placing the head joint at the spine's front end with forked eye bladders and a vane sail, adding a trailing tail chain with an upward arc at the rear carrying rods, and setting up a mast joint for the wind sails.

Now I'm defining the spine as a tube running along z at the pivot height, with a lower keel and axle positioned below, plus a second cross-axle at each unit's pivot point mimicking the real Strandbeest mechanism.

I'm connecting these with A-frame struts from the spine down to the axle ends on both sides, forming rigid triangular braces, and adding fixed link rods between the pivot and crank axle positions to lock the frame geometry together.

I'm abandoning the straight-rail approach since the A-frame struts don't align across units, and instead considering lower side rails that connect the pivot axle ends between adjacent units along the z-axis.

Now I'm planning diagonal bracing from the spine top of each unit to the pivot axle end of the next unit for triangulation, and setting the spine height and length along the z-axis. For the bladders, I'm thinking of laying 2-liter bottle shapes along z above the spine, lathed with a neck, shoulder, body, and base, colored translucent white.

For the head, I'm attaching two large eye-shaped bottle spheres near the front of the spine, white-toned with decal planes for eyes, mounted via forked supports.

I'm fixing the eye placement so it sits just outside the sphere surface instead of embedded. Now I'm figuring out the mast height and position, then sketching a triangular sail rigged between the mast and a boom.

Defining sail geometry...

For the pennant I'll extrude a thin triangular flag with solid blue paint plus a wave emblem texture plane on top. For the tail, I'm building a curving chain of tapered rods from the spine rear sweeping up and back, with a triangular fin sail extruded at the very end, joined by a bone at the tail.

Now for small details like zip ties, I'm placing tiny black tori along the spine, rotating each torus geometry so its ring axis aligns with the tangent direction of the spine sweep at each point.

For the feet, I want paint that fades toward sandy tones near the floor with noise streaks for grime, plus sun-fading on the upper surfaces. I'm also settling on a color palette: yellow paint for the main body, dark black for nodes, grayish metal for the axle, tan rope color, dark foot color, and blue for the cap.

For texture work, I'm sketching an eye SVG with a white base, ink outline, blue iris and highlights, plus considering a wave spiral emblem for the sail done in indigo on cream. I'm wary of using decal placement on the sail membrane since its return type is uncertain, so instead I'll bake the emblem directly into the sail's paint function.

Writing ring pattern logic...

I'm settling on textures beyond the sails: an eye, pennant, plate label reading "STRANDBEEST ✕ 07" on a yellow tag, and a bottle label wrapped by height. For the pennant I'm setting up a card frame at the mast top that extends backward along the flow axis so it reads like a flag trailing off the mast.

I'm working through the plane orientation for the pennant, placing it with a double-sided texture so it reads correctly whether viewed from the front or back, while checking how the drawing's left/right maps to the plane's facing direction so it doesn't appear mirrored.

Rather than fight the mirroring issue, I'll keep the pennant symmetric with no text so orientation doesn't matter, and skip labeling the mirrored side. I'll put a simple identifying plate—"ANIMARIS"—on the front-facing head crossbar where it reads correctly unmirrored, using a bold sans-serif font in the SVG. Now moving on to listing out the joints starting with the hips at the root.

Defining leg chains and crank joints...

I'll root hips at the origin along the spine and chain the parent relationship from there, then attach a head joint pointing outward from the last spine segment. I'm also considering adding a separate jaw joint parented to the head for added articulation, like a hinge beneath the skull.

For the head itself, I'm laying out eye spheres on either side, a forward-pointing beak shape made from a lathe cone, and a forked rod jaw sitting slightly below and forward of the head center.

I'm now moving to the implementation, setting up imports from the builder library and sketching out which utility functions I'll rely on—things like rng, polyline, catmull, bezier, paint, and mix—to construct the geometry.

For the yellow paint shader, I'm layering noise-driven color variations: a base yellow-gold mix, a sun-bleached highlight toward the top, scuff marks from high-frequency noise, and additional weathering blended near the bottom.

Now I'm turning to the bottle, planning its paint function with a lathe profile defined by height along the axis -- establishing a label band region with a bluish tint and white stripe details, then starting to sketch the outline coordinates (radius vs. height) for the bottle's shape.

Still writing outline points...

For the cap, I'm thinking of a separate colored cylinder part positioned at the neck's top, oriented along the bottle's axis, and sketching out a `bottle(at, dir, scale, capColor)` function that lathes the profile and attaches the cap as its own piece.

Now I'm working on bottle orientation—alternating neck direction (forward/back along z) between bottles by flipping the axis and adjusting the base position accordingly. Then I'm moving to sail membranes, planning a `membrane` helper that takes two edges and generates a grid of panels with configurable rows/columns and thickness for the sail shape.

For the mainsail, I'm defining the mast as a straight edge from the base to the top, paired with a curved catmull-rom edge representing the sail's leech, making sure both edges resample evenly by arc length despite differing lengths. For the jib, I'm setting up a similar mast-line edge and starting to define its second curved edge.

Writing sail paint function...

Adding rigging, mast, and boom geometry...

Attaching the fin as a small leaf-shaped extrusion near the tail tip, bound to the last tail joint and painted skin-colored. Now I'm working out the axle and frame geometry per leg unit, computing z-centers and leg extents from the base positions.

Checking the overall body length comes out around 5.4 meters, which feels too long for the creature I want, so I'm shrinking the scale factor and spacing to bring total height to roughly 2.4 and adjusting the tail and spine positions back inward.

I'm now working through lateral leg bar placement and double-checking whether the leg bars cross through the chassis crank axle near point O, since the A-Q-C bars sit close to that region and could overlap.

Checking unit 0 and unit 1's leg extents along z to make sure they don't collide given their different lateral plane offsets, then moving on to solving for the minimum foot height.

I need to find the ground offset by taking the minimum y across all nodes, not just the foot, since D could be lowest at some phases but C might dip lower at others. I'll set the ground plane using the minimum node y times scale plus a small margin, then place the foot sphere so it sinks only slightly below ground, well within tolerance.

Then I'm assigning spine y-position relative to the ground, and working out which bone each rod belongs to for the leg chain -- hip bone covers the upper rods near P, A, B, Q, C, while knee bone covers the lower rods toward D and the foot tip. Now I'm setting up the side plane offsets and starting to write the coordinate transform code for each point.

Writing crank, axle, and phase code...

There's a minor visual intersection between the strut and the plane region near the bottom, but it's acceptable since real structures have similar overlaps. I'm also adding longitudinal diagonal rods connecting the spine top to the outer pivot axle ends, plus fixed links between P and O at each plane center.

For the pivot structure, I'm planning small black cylinder nodes at points A, B, C, and Q in each plane, skipping redundant nodes at P and O since the axle already spans through there. The foot gets a simple dark sphere, flat shaded, without extra decoration.

Now I'm placing bottles along the deck in two rows flanking the spine at x=±0.17, spacing their z-positions to clear the mast and sail while keeping the boom height above them.

I'm trying to figure out a good spot to mount the name plate — considering the gap between the eyes, the jaw area, and finally settling on attaching it flat to the front face of the mast near its base.

Still working out eye placement...

I'm designing the eye decal with a blue-green iris, pupil, highlights, and a dark eyelid line, blending against a warm-white sphere. For the beak, I'm positioning the upper and lower jaw pieces as forward-pointing bottle shapes near the head, adjusting their offsets so the cap tips don't overlap.

Now I'm checking the jaw hinge geometry, making sure the gap between the upper and lower bottle shapes is small enough to look connected once scaled down, and placing the eye spheres relative to the head joint—though I'm noticing the eyes might overlap with the upper beak bottle at certain x-ranges, so I need to adjust their position to avoid intersection.

Writing helper functions...

Still defining joints and lathe geometry...

Adjusting cap position slightly to sit properly on the neck, and allowing non-spine bones like the head to be passed in. For the bottle's paint, I'm coloring bands based on vertical position—blue for the label area, pale cyan-white elsewhere with noise, darker near the base.

For ropes, I'm deciding between a simple two-point sweep and a rod helper with flat ends, or adding a slight catenary sag using a catmull curve for a more natural droop. For the pennant, I'm sketching an SVG with a swallow-tail shape in red with a wave emblem and sun circle inside, then sizing plane geometry to match it.

Now I'm working out the pennant's placement at the mast top, positioning the two-sided planes slightly offset from the mast center so each faces outward correctly, and checking that the hoist edge aligns toward the mast while accounting for how the mirrored side reads from a viewer facing the opposite direction.

This reveals that the simple mirrored-offset approach fails geometrically -- for the -x side the drawing ends up reversed, putting the swallowtail near the mast instead of the hoist. So I decide to generate two separate textures, creating a flipped version of the pennant SVG via a horizontal scale transform so each side reads correctly. I'm also sketching a wavy emblem path for the pennant graphic and a dark rounded plate SVG with cream border and text for a nameplate design.

I'm now shifting to the tail fin geometry, defining its extrusion outline as a set of 2D points and figuring out orientation vectors, thickness, color, and which bone joint to attach it to, then laying out the tail's 3D spine points with increasing height and depth to create a tapered sweep.

I'm then sketching the hierarchy: hips joint at the base, spine chain parented to hips, mast joint parented into the spine's second segment, and matching up z-coordinates for each spine joint so the mast sits correctly within its span. I note that I need to compute leg positions and the derived y-offset before actually constructing the joints, since the build order matters.

Now I'm laying out the leg chains per side, using a sign-based naming scheme (L/R) and lane offsets for each leg joint, with parenting handled via nearest-joint lookup on the spine. I decide to skip extra decorative touches like a wind-spinner, anemometer, or bunting, keeping the design simpler, and move on to writing the full layout code.

Writing module scaffold and leg geometry...

Adding axle spans, collars, and crank rest rods, then wrapping up with final assembly before writing the sail.

Now I'm defining the stay and shroud ropes connecting the mast top to the tail and head points, and the shroud lines down to the pivot axle ends, using nearest-joint lookups for rope bone attachments before writing everything out.
